But here we are, in a world where Damon broke the critics and box office\'s neck with his bare hands, stabbing them with a pen and beating them to death with a book. Astonishingly well-shot action, real-world stakes and a withering contempt for Bond\'s slickness and womanising combine to give the Noughties an action hero to be proud of. Weakest link? Unusually, the first one is generally considered the weakest – although only in comparison to Paul Greengrass\'s frantic, frenetic follow-ups. Fun fact: When Bourne looks in the mirror and says something in foreign at the beginning of The Bourne Identity , he\'s speaking Dutch. Read Empire \'s reviews of The Bourne Identity , Supremacy and Ultimatum . See if any of them made it our list of the best action movies . 5. The Godfather Trilogy (1972 – 1990) The Godfather (1972) | The Godfather: Part II (1974) | The Godfather: Part III (1990) Streaming on: Paramount+ | Apple TV Director: Francis Ford Coppola Starring: Al Pacino , Marlon Brando, Robert de Niro, Diane Keaton, James Caan, Robert Duvall, Talia Shire, John Cazale, Andy Garcia, Sofia Coppola, Eli Wallach, Joe Mantegna Francis Ford Coppola\'s epic adaptation of Mario Puzo\'s equally epic book was a perfect marriage of director and subject. Coming from a large Italian-American family himself, Coppola understood the novel\'s themes about family, immigration and the American dream on a profound level, and just had to add a ladle of crime and assassination to bring the mix to boil. Part II expertly layered past and present in a brilliant expansion and clarification of the world, while Part III , whatever its faults, completes the arc for Michael Corleone (Al Pacino), as he faces the consequences of the choices he\'s made and watches the next generation grow up. Weakest link? Altogether now! The Godfather: Part III ! In retrospect everyone agrees that Sofia Coppola is a better director than Corleone offspring, and while the third film has its defenders, no one would seriously claim it\'s up to the standard of the previous two. Fun fact: Originally Winona Ryder was set to play Sofia Coppola\'s role – but backed out to appear in Edward Scissorhands . Read Empire \'s reviews of The Godfather , Part II and Part III . See where Part II came in our list of the 10 best Robert de Niro movies . Find out what our readers voted as the best Godfather moments across the trilogy. 4. Toy Story 1-3 (1995 – 2010) Toy Story (1995) | Toy Story 2 (1999) | Toy Story 3 (2010) Streaming on: Disney+ Directors: John Lasster, Lee Unkrich Starring: Tom Hanks, Tim Allen, Joan Cusack, Don Rickles, Wallace Shawn, John Ratzenberger, Estelle Harris, Blake Clark The release of the first Toy Story film was anticipated chiefly from a technological point of view, as the first entirely computer-animated film ever made. It was only as word from screenings leaked out that it became clear that this was also a storytelling milestone, a blast of fresh air to a moribund animation industry and one that took the world by storm. Incredibly, the sequel lived up to that standard, with Empire calling it an "upgrade" to the original – and even more improbably, the third instalment, fought over and delayed for years, became another triumph. Flawless characterisation, spot-on voice work and the relentless quest for perfection in both story and look may now just be standard practice for Pixar, but it\'s worth remembering how special that is. Weakest link? You could try to pick holes in them, but honestly, why bother? They\'re all consistently excellent. Fun fact: Lee Unkrich, who directed the third film, was an editor on the first and a co-director on the second. Read Empire \'s reviews of Toy Story , Toy Story 2 and Toy Story 3 . See where they came in our lists of the best animated movies , best kids movies , and Pixar movie ranking . 3. Back To The Future Trilogy (1985 – 1990) Back To The Future (1985) | Back To The Future Part II (1989) | Back To The Future Part III (1990) Streaming on: Netflix | Prime Video Director: Robert Zemeckis Starring: Michael J. Fox, Christopher Lloyd, Crispin Glover, Lea Thompson, Thomas F. Wilson, Claudia Wells, Elizabeth Shue, Mary Steenbergen Show us a person who doesn\'t like Back To The Future and we\'ll show you a person who is tired of life. The Zemeckis-directed, Spielberg-produced time-travelling tale of Marty McFly races along at, oooh, around 88mph, fuelled by plutonium and Fox\'s career-making, insanely charming performance as an average teen thrust 30 years back in time. Part II was a twisty, turny paradox-spinning puzzler, followed by a gorgeous mix of old West and space age in Part III . Consistently fun, funny and about as good an adventure romp as you could wish for, there\'s a reason that this is still wildly popular decades on. Weakest link? Funnily enough, conventional wisdom at the time tended to rate the second film lowest (as reflected by Empire \'s reviews) but nowadays you\'ll find more people slagging off the third. It all smacks of looking a gift horse in the mouth to us though. Fun fact: Once upon a time, the time machine was going to be a fridge. Spielberg and Zemeckis nixed the idea because they were worried about kids copying the movie and getting trapped in old fridges. Read Empire \'s reviews of Back To The Future , Part II and Part III . 2. The Original Star Wars Trilogy (1977 – 1983) Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope (1977) | Star Wars: Episode V - The Empire Strikes Back (1980) | Star Wars: Episode VI - Return of the Jedi (1983) Streaming on: Disney+ Directors: George Lucas, Irvin Kershner, Richard Marquand Starring: Mark Hamill, Harrison Ford, Carrie Fisher, Alec Guinness, Peter Cushing, Anthony Daniels, Peter Mayhew, Kenny Baker, David Prowse, James Earl Jones, Billy Dee Williams, Jeremy Bulloch George Lucas\' opening space-opera salvo changed the filmmaking landscape, energised a generation and set an impossible standard for any sequel. Irvin Kershner\'s sequel , with Lucas overseeing, delivered something even bigger and better, and also gave us perhaps the most famous twist in cinema history. And the third, while it may have cutesy teddy bears taking down an Empire, also has a series of fantastic action scenes, from the fight with the Rancor to the lightsaber battle on the Death Star – itself under attack from outside. The original batch of Star Wars movies is a triple-whammy that has spawned imitators, prequels, endless other media permutations and even a religion. How many trilogies can claim that? Weakest link? Most of the fanboys would have you believe it\'s Jedi , but that\'s got some of the trilogy\'s best bits in it, and – whatever they claim – no one hated the Ewoks, even when they were a kid. Fun fact: Pop quiz, hotshot. Who has the last line in New Hope? Answer: Chewbacca. Read Empire \'s reviews of A New Hope , The Empire Strikes Back and Return Of The Jedi . 1. The Lord Of The Rings (2001 – 2003) The Lord Of The Rings: The Fellowship Of The Ring (2001) | The Lord Of The Rings: The Two Towers (2002) | The Lord Of The Rings: The Return Of The King (2003) Streaming on: Apple TV | Prime Video Director: Peter Jackson Starring: Elijah Wood, Viggo Mortensen, Ian McKellen, Cate Blanchett, Sean Astin, Sean Bean, John Rhys-Davies, Christopher Lee, Andy Serkis, Orlando Bloom, Dominic Monahan, Billy Boyd, Liv Tyler, Hugo Weaving, Miranda Otto, Karl Urban, David Wenham, Bernard Hill, Ian Holm, Brad Dourif, John Noble Peter Jackson\'s stunning trilogy, filmed back-to-back and released in the form of Christmas presents for three consecutive years, just pipped Star Wars to the top of the poll. Why? Well, there\'s the painstaking attention to detail (characters even had their coats-of-arms emblazoned on the never-seen linings of their costumes for maximum authenticity), New Zealand scenery so breathtaking you can feel the wind on your face, the pitch-perfect casting and the huge-scale effects. In the end, however, it all comes down to friendship, and fellowship, and a struggle against the odds (or, if you will, orcs). It\'s the fact that Peter Jackson was able to keep his eye on the emotion even while the spectacle swirled around him that makes these three films such a stunning achievement – and why all three of them appear in our official list of the 100 greatest movies of all time . Weakest link? There really isn\'t one – although a few people gripe about Return Of The King \'s extended endings. Fun fact: While Return Of The King is tied with Titanic and Ben-Hur for the Most Oscars For A Single Film record (that\'d be 11), it\'s notable for winning all the Academy Awards it was nominated for, which neither of the others managed to do. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian Theatre Ivo van Hove’s All My Sons extends the UK’s special relationship with Arthur Miller In his first hit play, now receiving another starry revival, the celebrated dramatist’s analysis of the American psyche is steeped in European tradition Michael Billington Tue 11 Nov 2025 04.24 EST Last modified on Tue 11 Nov 2025 06.24 EST Share T he British theatre’s long love affair with Arthur Miller continues. This week sees the start of previews for Ivo van Hove’s production of Miller’s first Broadway hit, All My Sons, which has had half a dozen major revivals over the past five decades. Indeed, you could argue that Miller is more honoured here than at home. On his death it was said in the Times Literary Supplement: “He was mourned in England as a revered contemporary, in America as a figure from a bygone age.” Why this division? One answer, supplied by All My Sons, is that Miller analysed the American psyche while being steeped in European tradition. It is difficult to discuss this particular play without giving away the plot. It is, however, an open secret that it hinges on the unproven accusation that Joe Keller, as a wartime manufacturer of aircraft engines, allowed faulty cylinder heads to be dispatched to the air force knowing they could endanger life. Immediately this makes one think of Ibsen. In The Pillars of Society, rarely seen these days , a wealthy shipowner allows his detested brother-in-law to go to sea in a rotten vessel only to discover that his own son is also on board. In his brilliant book on Miller’s plays, Christopher Bigsby also references The Wild Duck and sees in Joe’s son, Chris, an embodiment of the flawed idealist comparable to Ibsen’s Gregers Werle. But Bigsby hits the nail on the head when he says that Miller, exactly like Ibsen, blends the tragic and the comic and shows the present for ever haunted by the past. View image in fullscreen Present haunted by the past … Bill Pullman, Colin Morgan, Sally Field and Jenna Coleman in the 2019 production of All My Sons at the Old Vic. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian While Miller is clearly indebted to Ibsen, he is also a profoundly American writer. I once had the temerity to ask him, in the course of a public interview about his autobiography, Timebends, whether he had ever considered relocating to Europe since at home he had endured political persecution and critical hostility. I remember Miller looking faintly aghast at the idea and stressing his commitment to his native land. No American critic has written better about this than Harold Clurman who, in his review of the original 1947 production of All My Sons, made a vital distinction between a play’s material and its meaning, and saw in Miller “a moral talent with a passionate persistence that resembles that of the New England preacher who fashioned our first American rhetoric”. Given that All My Sons is Ibsenite and American, how does one stage it? Looking back at three past productions, I am struck by their social realism and strong performances. Michael Blakemore’s 1981 production, also at Wyndham’s, stressed the play’s folksy back-yard humour and was expertly played, with Colin Blakely lending Joe a stocky muscularity and Rosemary Harris investing his wife, Kate, with the look of a blooming martyr. View image in fullscreen Stark … Mark Strong, centre, in A View from the Bridge by Arthur Miller at Young Vic in 2014, directed by Ivo van Hove. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian Howard Davies, who had first directed the play at the National in 2000, did an even better production in the West End in 2010 with David Suchet, like Blakely, stressing Joe’s back-yard bonhomie and Zoë Wanamaker subtly suggesting that Kate was as swathed in pretence as her husband. Arthur Miller: ‘My legacy? Some good parts for actors’ Read more More recently, in 2019, Jeremy Herrin directed it at the Old Vic with two American actors in the lead: Bill Pullman as a strenuously self-justifying Joe, and Sally Field, encasing herself in her cardigan as if it were a protective shield, as a superb Kate. So what can we expect from Van Hove? Given that in his celebrated 2014 Young Vic revival of A View from the Bridge he dispensed with Red Hook realism to stage the play in a stark black box, I doubt we will get an Ohio back yard that looks as if it were a Norman Rockwell cover for an American magazine. With Bryan Cranston as Joe, and Marianne Jean-Baptiste and Paapa Essiedu as Kate and Chris, we can also expect a fresh take on the Keller family. But, however it turns out, I hope the production recognises that Miller is a deeply American moralist with a bias to the European past, from Aeschylus to Ibsen. By Michele Debczak , Anastasia Rose Hyden | Share on Facebook Share on X Copy Article A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving - Food | PeanutsOnline Share on Facebook Share on X Share on Reddit Copy Article After finishing your October horror movie marathon , you may be tempted to dive right into Elf (2003), some Rankin Bass holiday specials, and Itâ\x80\x99s a Wonderful Life (1946). But thereâ\x80\x99s a whole category of cinema to watch between the Halloween and Christmas seasons that viewers often ignore. What makes a Thanksgiving movie isnâ\x80\x99t always clear-cutâ\x80\x94some are conceived around the holiday, and others feature one memorable scene with a turkey on the table. Like the holiday itself, Thanksgiving movies are the offbeat, sometimes melodramatic stepsiblings to their Christmas counterparts. If youâ\x80\x99re looking for something other than football or parade coverage to watch on the holiday, check out the Thanksgiving (or Thanksgiving- ish ) films below.Â Addams Family Values (1993) Planes, Trains, and Automobiles (1987) The Last Waltz (1978) Miracle on 34th Street (1947) Pieces of April (2003) The Ice Storm (1997) The House of Yes (1997) Kristy (2014) A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving (1973) Sheâ\x80\x99s Gotta Have It (1986) Spider-Man (2002) Youâ\x80\x99ve Got Mail (1998) Mistress America (2015) The Humans (2021) Scent of a Woman (1992) Home for the Holidays (1995) The Gold Rush (1925) Prisoners (2013) Addams Family Values (1993) If youâ\x80\x99re still in the mood for something spooky after Halloween, Addams Family Values (1993) is the ideal transitional film. The sequel features Anjelica Houston, Raul Julia, Christina Ricci, and Christopher Lloyd reprising their roles as the titular family , with Joan Cusack and David Krumholtz playing memorable new characters. The plot isnâ\x80\x99t Thanksgiving-centric, but one scene in particular makes it a great film to watch around the holiday. While reenacting the first Thanksgiving at camp, Wednesday Addams breaks from the script and delivers a speech listing the injustices Native Americans have endured since the pilgrims arrived. It ends with the line: â\x80\x9cAnd for all these reasons, I have decided to scalp you and burn your village to the ground.â\x80\x9d Itâ\x80\x99s the perfect antidote to the feel-good content flooding airwaves this time of year. Planes, Trains, and Automobiles (1987) This 1987 comedy focuses on the lead-up to Thanksgiving rather than the meal itself. Steve Martin plays a marketing executive who is desperately trying to make it home to his family for Thanksgiving while dealing with the antics of a shower curtain ring salesman played by John Candy . The film also marks an early foray into holiday movies for writer John Hughes, who penned Home Alone (1990) a few years later.Â You May Also Like ... 8 Coziest Fall Movies of All Time 15 Must-See Holiday Horror Movies How Schmaltzy Hallmark Christmas Movies Came to Rule the Holiday Season Add Mental Floss as aÂ preferred news source ! The Last Waltz (1978) This legendary documentary not only chronicles the history of The Band, but also captures their final concert, which took place on Thanksgiving Day, November 25, 1976. They were joined by special guests like Bob Dylan , Joni Mitchell, Muddy Waters, Ringo Starr, and Neil Young. On top of featuring one of the greatest musical lineups of all time, the flick was also the first of many collaborations between The Band frontman Robbie Robertson and director Martin Scorsese . Robertson acted as a musical consultant for multiple future Scorsese films, including Raging Bull and The Wolf of Wall Street . He also composed the scores for The Color of Money, The Irishman , and Killers of the Flower Moon , among others. Miracle on 34th Street (1947) If youâ\x80\x99re feeling more festive than spooky in the days between the Halloween and Christmas seasons, put on Miracle on 34th Street . While itâ\x80\x99s generally considered a classic Christmas movie, the film opens with Edmund Gwenn as Santa Claus riding in the Macyâ\x80\x99s Thanksgiving Day Parade , so it has a foot planted in both holidays. Fun fact: Gwenn really did play Santa in the parade in 1946, and that scene consists of actual footage from the event. Pieces of April (2003) After she learns that her mother (Patricia Clarkson) has terminal cancer, black sheep April (Katie Holmes) offers to host Thanksgiving for her estranged suburban family in her rundown Lower East Side apartment, a prospect that doesnâ\x80\x99t excite them. This indie dramedy, which was filmed over just 16 days, was made on a budget of just $300,000 but went on to gross over $3.2 million and it perfectly captures the stresses of the holidays, especially as everything goes awry. The Ice Storm (1997) Christina Ricci also appears in Ang Leeâ\x80\x99s The Ice Storm â\x80\x94 another movie that features an acidic Thanksgiving speech. Over the course of the holiday break in the 1970s, a Connecticut family is pulled apart by alcohol, sexual experimentation, and an extramarital affair. Things come to a head at Thanksgiving dinner, when family matriarch Wendy (played by Joan Allen) thanks the lord for â\x80\x9cletting us white people kill all the Indians and steal their tribal lands. And stuff ourselves like pigs, even though children in Asia are being napalmed.â\x80\x9d The House of Yes (1997) No matter how screwed up your family is, they probably look like the Waltons or Cleavers next to the Pascal clan. Mrs. Pascal (GeneviÃ¨ve Bujold) is implied to have murdered her husband; Anthony (Freddie Prinze Jr.) is a sexual predator; and twins Marty (John Hamilton) and Jackie (Parker Posey in an acclaimed performance) were embroiled in an incestuous relationship until he moved away from home. When Marty brings his fiancÃ©e Lesly (Tori Spelling) home for Thanksgiving, she gets caught up in the familyâ\x80\x99s insanity against her will. Depending on your appreciation for black humor, The House of Yes might make you laughâ\x80\x94or cringeâ\x80\x94but at the very least, youâ\x80\x99ll probably be thankful that youâ\x80\x99re not a Pascal.Â Kristy (2014) There can be worse things than spending Thanksgiving with your family. If youâ\x80\x99re a student hunkering down on campus instead of schlepping home for the festivities, you might want to check out this horror flick. Unlike most of her classmates at an elite private university, scholarship student Justine (Ashley Greene) cannot afford to return home to spend the season with her family, so she opts to stay at her nearly deserted school. Unfortunately, she becomes the target of a cult of ritualistic killers and is forced to fight for her life. A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving (1973) Watching the Peanuts holiday specials is an annual tradition in many households. A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving (1973) isnâ\x80\x99t quite as iconic as Itâ\x80\x99s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966) or A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965), but itâ\x80\x99s still a seasonal classic. Sheâ\x80\x99s Gotta Have It (1986) Spike Leeâ\x80\x99s first feature-length film follows Nola (Tracy Camilla Johns), an unapologetically confident woman juggling simultaneous relationships with three very different men. The film hits its crescendo when she invites all three to Thanksgiving dinner, and itâ\x80\x99s a great flick to throw on if you're hosting Friendsgiving for adults only. Sheâ\x80\x99s Gotta Have It features the first appearance of Mars Blackmon (played by Lee), a basketball fanatic and collector of Air Jordan sneakers . Lee would reprise the character in a popular series of commercials for the shoes in the 1980s and 1990s. Spider-Man (2002) Sam Raimiâ\x80\x99s original Spider-Man has one of the superhero genreâ\x80\x99s best ensembles, and the cast is at its best during the filmâ\x80\x99s Thanksgiving scene. You have Peter Parker (Tobey Maguire) quipping about cranberry sauce; Norman Osborn (Willem Dafoe) letting his inner goblin come through while carving the turkey; and Aunt May (Rosemary Harris) trying to keep everyone on their best behavior. The movie also features a parade set piece. The best Spidey villains have, obviously, been featured heavily in the live-action films. Whether it's in the Sam Raimi trilogy, the Marc Webb duology, or the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Peter Parker has faced some extremely powerful villains throughout his cinematic career. If the Wall-Crawler beat his foes right off the bat, then audiences wouldn't have entertaining movies to go see. The hero will always get his butt whooped by his villains at some point in the story, because he can't win every fight. Thus, Spidey has had some pretty rough beatings across the years, but who's given him the worst —physically and non-physically? Whether they've killed the love of his life or almost killed him in an intense hand-to-hand battle, Spidey's villains have always given him a run for his money. 12 The Rhino (Paul Giamatti) Paul Giamatti as The Rhino in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 Image via Sony Pictures Releasing People were incredibly excited when they saw the walking wrecking ball known as The Rhino ( Paul Giamatti ) in the trailer for The Amazing Spider-Man 2 . Facing off with such a gigantic foe makes for a perfect David and Goliath-type story for the Web-Slinger, which always leads to great fight scenes. Unfortunately for Rhino fans, he doesn't affect Spider-Man ( Andrew Garfield ) in the slightest. In all fairness, this version of The Rhino shoots some missiles at Spider-Man in the one scene where his armor appears, which also happens to be the final scene of The Amazing Spider-Man 2 . The two don't even touch each other, with the film ending on a cliffhanger, implying that they were about to fight. Pretty disappointing, honestly, but it is what it is. 11 Harry Osborn (James Franco) Harry Osborn on a glider stopping in mid-air in Spider-Man 3 Image via Sony Pictures Entertainment The conflict between Peter Parker ( Tobey Maguire ) and Harry Osborn ( James Franco ) was set up and built upon ever since the end of the first Spider-Man film, when Harry vowed to make Spider-Man pay for what he did to his dad. Obviously, this meant that the two best friends were going to meet some heavy conflict eventually, and it all came to a climax in the trilogy-capper , Spider-Man 3 . At the start of Spider-Man 3 , Harry takes on the mantle of his father's persona, the Green Goblin—commonly called New Goblin outside of the film—to kill Peter once and for all. Driven mad by vengeance and anger, the fight he has with Pete after Mary Jane Watson's ( Kirsten Dunst ) play is intense and fast-paced. However, it is the only time he faces off with his ex-best pal, and this Goblin Jr. doesn't beat Spidey much , being taken down swiftly. 10 Shocker ( Bokeem Woodbine) Herman Schultz scheming in in Spider-Man: Homecoming Image via Sony Pictures Releasing In the MCU, Shocker ( Bokeem Woodbine ) is a pretty underrated Spider-Man villain . He faces off with the hero ( Tom Holland ) only once, but he actually really smacks Spidey around. Shocker punches Spidey so hard that he flies through a bus , before hitting him with another. Peter tries his best, but getting hit by a full school bus didn't do his brain any favors. In fact, the arachnid is about to be taken down until Ned Leeds ( Jacob Batalon ) comes in for the save, using one of the hero's web shooters to stop Shocker from killing his pal. Despite being just a guy with some punching tech, Shocker really smacks Spider-Man around and deserves to make a bigger and better comeback. 9 The Lizard (Rhys Ifans) The Lizard from The Amazing Spider-Man Image via Sony Pictures Releasing When thinking about it, it's pretty understandable that a gigantic mutated lizard man would be someone to kick around a superhero pretty well. While The Amazing Spider-Man let a lot of fans down with its depiction of The Lizard ( Rhys Ifans ), he still gets some good licks on the Wall-Crawler. In the comics, Lizard is typically more savage and brutal, which is missing in his live-action appearances. However, whenever he faces off with Spider-Man, the Lizard never really gets beaten , aside from his retreat in the fight at Midtown High School. The grotesque villain runs away from the bridge because the serum is running out, and Spider-Man escapes their conflict when in the sewers. In fact, the Lizard only loses the fight on the rooftop because Peter beats him to the punch in stopping his plans. 8 The Vulture (Michael Keaton) Vulture smiling while holding a knife in Spider-Man: Homecoming. Image via Sony Pictures Releasing Something Spider-Man has over most of his villains is his agility and ability to swing around and take to the skies. What happens when a villain arises who practically owns the skies? Vulture ( Michael Keaton ) was the perfect villain to kick off Spider-Man's solo career in the MCU, being a lethal threat, but not big enough for the likes of Iron Man ( Robert Downey Jr. ) to notice. Thus, Spidey is the only person who can take the bad bird down. His talons can rip into Spider-Man, his wings can snap his web threads, and his speed allows him to catch the hero off guard, as it happens during their final confrontation on the beach. The Vulture beats Holland's Peter multiple times . Not only does Venom not set off the Wall-Crawler's Spider-Sense, but he's just as fast (if not faster) and just as strong . The best way to describe Venom is Spider-Man is he was evil , which is a horrific thing to think about. Had it not been for Harry Osborn's sacrifice to save him, Peter would have most likely died at the hands of Venom . The symbiote may have only fought Spidey once, but he makes his mark and ensures himself as a memorable villain for reasons that aren't exclusively bad. Venim is ruthless as he almost kills Peter, almost kills Mary Jane, and unfortunately takes Harry's life. 6 Sandman ( Thomas Haden Church) Thomas Haden Church as Sandman in Spider-Man 3 Image via Sony Pictures Releasing The ability to absorb all of the sand in the area surrounding you, turning you into a gigantic, multiple-story monster, is pretty dang overpowered. Sandman, with the help of Venom, was mere moments away from taking Spider-Man's life by simply using one hand and slamming down on him. He literally stood there and hit Spider-Man like a whack-a-mole, barely breaking a sweat . Being able to kill someone with that much ease is freaky, and if not for Harry Osborn, the Sandman would have squashed Spidey like one does to an actual spider. 5 Electro (Jamie Foxx) Image via Sony Pictures Releasing While he gets a lot of flak, thanks to The Amazing Spider-Man 2 's overall weak rep, Electro ( Jamie Foxx ) is a pretty dang powerful villain, and the movie doesn't shy away from that. Electro can zap Spidey away with a mere touch and has the ability to control anything with electricity. Not to mention, his electrical blasts are so powerful, they evaporated civilians in Times Square during his first fight with Spider-Man. The power of electricity is extremely strong; after all, it's a basic law of the world. It doesn't take a lot of electricity to shut down the human body completely, and while Spider-Man has an enhanced physicality, even he can't take a bolt of lightning to the chest and just walk it off. This vulnerability is proven throughout the entire final fight, in which Spidey's plans to stop Electro would not have been possible without Gwen Stacy ( Emma Stone ) there. Even so, the arachnid gets mere seconds away from frying his whole body while trying to hold his webs together. Before Gwen arrives, Spider-Man is at Electro's mercy and is getting his world rocked for almost the entire fight . 4 Doctor Otto Octavius (Alfred Molina) There's no questioning that Doctor Otto Octavius ( Alfred Molina ), aka Doctor Octopus, is the villain of one of the best superhero movies, Spider-Man 2 , which would make him one of the de facto best Spider-Man villains. Alongside that reputation, Doc Ock also gave the Wall-Crawler several major beatings. Pete only bests Otto in battle once , at the end of the movie, after being beaten or having the villain escape in the previous ones. Doc Ock almost fully crushes Spidey's head like a watermelon in the bank fight, almost kills Aunt May ( Rosemary Harris ) , and almost impales the hero if not for her interference. In the iconic train battle, Spidey gets smacked around until Otto forces him to stay behind to keep the train from crashing, causing Peter to extend himself to a limit that could have easily killed him. He also captures the Web-Slinger, something that not many have done. Not to forget, in the film's extended cut, Spider-Man 2.1 , he even puts the hero in front of an oncoming train , which he gets hit by. 3 Harry Osborn (Dane DeHaan) Dane DeHaan as Green Goblin in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 Image via Sony Pictures Releasing Another negatively-received villain from the live-action franchises is yet another Harry Osborn ( Dane DeHaan ), this time from The Amazing Spider-Man universe. Appearing pretty much out of nowhere after the final Electro fight in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 , this Harry-Goblin puts up quite a fight against Peter when he brings him and Gwen Stacy to the clock tower for a close-quarters battle. Not only is it an extremely tough battle, but this Goblin Jr. beats Peter in a way that no other villain has: he takes the life of Gwen Stacy by holding the arachnid down and forcing the web holding her to snap. This action is so impactful—so terribly ruinous—that it puts Spider-Man out of commission for months. From sweeping fantasy epics to gritty crime sagas the best movie trilogies represent storytelling at its most ambitious and satisfying. These aren\'t just three films released one after the other – they\'re carefully constructed narrative arcs that build worlds, explore core themes, and deliver emotional payoffs that single films simply can\'t match. The greatest film trilogies work because they understand the classic three-act storytelling structure: the introduction, the escalation, and the resolution. Whether it\'s watching a young farmboy become a Jedi Knight across a galaxy far, far away, following a teenager\'s adventures through time and space, or witnessing the rise and fall of a mafia family across generations, the best trilogy movies give us room to breathe, grow attached, and experience genuine transformation alongside their characters. From the action-packed thrills of globe-trotting archaeologists and time-travelling DeLoreans to intimate character studies from auteur filmmakers, movie trilogies span every genre and filmmaking approach imaginable. What makes certain trilogies endure while others fade? Sometimes it\'s the visionary director who maps out all three chapters from the start. Other times, it\'s the unexpected alchemy of a sequel that deepens what came before, transforming a standalone hit into something greater. And occasionally, it\'s the cultural moment they capture – the way the best trilogies of all time become iconic texts for entire generations, their quotes embedded in our conversations, their themes debated for decades. Like we said: it’s the magic number. How We Chose The Best Film Trilogies Compiling a definitive ranking of the best trilogies was never going to be a simple task. We started by asking you, Empire \'s passionate readers, to vote for your favourite all-time movie trilogies. Thousands of you responded, championing everything from pure three-film series untouched by prequels or sequels, to specific trios within longer franchises, to triptychs that were intended to be evaluated as a threesome even if they don’t share the same cast or characters. Where a coherent narrative across three films existed, we counted it – which is why you\'ll find certain trilogies here even when fourth or fifth instalments later emerged. Once your votes were in, we turned to Empire \'s experienced team of critics and contributors, asking them to weigh in with their expertise on the artistic merit, cultural impact, and lasting influence of each trilogy. We evaluated how well each trilogy functions as a complete narrative – does the third film stick the landing? Does the middle chapter avoid the sophomore slump? Do all three films come together to create something greater than the sum of their parts? After much heated discussion, countless rewatches, and vigorous debate about everything from superhero standouts to South Korean revenge thrillers, from comedy spoofs to zombie horrors , we arrived at our final ranking. Whether you\'re a devotee of groundbreaking sci-fi, animated classics or international arthouse cinema, you\'ll find something to love – and, probably, something to argue about – in our rundown of the greatest film trios ever made. So here, without further ado, is Empire \'s official ranking of the 33 (see what we did there?) best movie trilogies of all time... 33. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian Theatre Ivo van Hove’s All My Sons extends the UK’s special relationship with Arthur Miller In his first hit play, now receiving another starry revival, the celebrated dramatist’s analysis of the American psyche is steeped in European tradition Michael Billington Tue 11 Nov 2025 04.24 EST Last modified on Tue 11 Nov 2025 06.24 EST Share T he British theatre’s long love affair with Arthur Miller continues. This week sees the start of previews for Ivo van Hove’s production of Miller’s first Broadway hit, All My Sons, which has had half a dozen major revivals over the past five decades. Indeed, you could argue that Miller is more honoured here than at home. On his death it was said in the Times Literary Supplement: “He was mourned in England as a revered contemporary, in America as a figure from a bygone age.” Why this division? One answer, supplied by All My Sons, is that Miller analysed the American psyche while being steeped in European tradition. It is difficult to discuss this particular play without giving away the plot. It is, however, an open secret that it hinges on the unproven accusation that Joe Keller, as a wartime manufacturer of aircraft engines, allowed faulty cylinder heads to be dispatched to the air force knowing they could endanger life. Immediately this makes one think of Ibsen. In The Pillars of Society, rarely seen these days , a wealthy shipowner allows his detested brother-in-law to go to sea in a rotten vessel only to discover that his own son is also on board. In his brilliant book on Miller’s plays, Christopher Bigsby also references The Wild Duck and sees in Joe’s son, Chris, an embodiment of the flawed idealist comparable to Ibsen’s Gregers Werle. But Bigsby hits the nail on the head when he says that Miller, exactly like Ibsen, blends the tragic and the comic and shows the present for ever haunted by the past. View image in fullscreen Present haunted by the past … Bill Pullman, Colin Morgan, Sally Field and Jenna Coleman in the 2019 production of All My Sons at the Old Vic. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian While Miller is clearly indebted to Ibsen, he is also a profoundly American writer. I once had the temerity to ask him, in the course of a public interview about his autobiography, Timebends, whether he had ever considered relocating to Europe since at home he had endured political persecution and critical hostility. I remember Miller looking faintly aghast at the idea and stressing his commitment to his native land. No American critic has written better about this than Harold Clurman who, in his review of the original 1947 production of All My Sons, made a vital distinction between a play’s material and its meaning, and saw in Miller “a moral talent with a passionate persistence that resembles that of the New England preacher who fashioned our first American rhetoric”. Given that All My Sons is Ibsenite and American, how does one stage it? Looking back at three past productions, I am struck by their social realism and strong performances. Michael Blakemore’s 1981 production, also at Wyndham’s, stressed the play’s folksy back-yard humour and was expertly played, with Colin Blakely lending Joe a stocky muscularity and Rosemary Harris investing his wife, Kate, with the look of a blooming martyr. View image in fullscreen Stark … Mark Strong, centre, in A View from the Bridge by Arthur Miller at Young Vic in 2014, directed by Ivo van Hove. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian Howard Davies, who had first directed the play at the National in 2000, did an even better production in the West End in 2010 with David Suchet, like Blakely, stressing Joe’s back-yard bonhomie and Zoë Wanamaker subtly suggesting that Kate was as swathed in pretence as her husband. Arthur Miller: ‘My legacy? Some good parts for actors’ Read more More recently, in 2019, Jeremy Herrin directed it at the Old Vic with two American actors in the lead: Bill Pullman as a strenuously self-justifying Joe, and Sally Field, encasing herself in her cardigan as if it were a protective shield, as a superb Kate. So what can we expect from Van Hove? Given that in his celebrated 2014 Young Vic revival of A View from the Bridge he dispensed with Red Hook realism to stage the play in a stark black box, I doubt we will get an Ohio back yard that looks as if it were a Norman Rockwell cover for an American magazine. With Bryan Cranston as Joe, and Marianne Jean-Baptiste and Paapa Essiedu as Kate and Chris, we can also expect a fresh take on the Keller family. But, however it turns out, I hope the production recognises that Miller is a deeply American moralist with a bias to the European past, from Aeschylus to Ibsen. What makes a Thanksgiving movie isnâ\x80\x99t always clear-cutâ\x80\x94some are conceived around the holiday, and others feature one memorable scene with a turkey on the table. Like the holiday itself, Thanksgiving movies are the offbeat, sometimes melodramatic stepsiblings to their Christmas counterparts. If youâ\x80\x99re looking for something other than football or parade coverage to watch on the holiday, check out the Thanksgiving (or Thanksgiving- ish ) films below.Â Addams Family Values (1993) Planes, Trains, and Automobiles (1987) The Last Waltz (1978) Miracle on 34th Street (1947) Pieces of April (2003) The Ice Storm (1997) The House of Yes (1997) Kristy (2014) A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving (1973) Sheâ\x80\x99s Gotta Have It (1986) Spider-Man (2002) Youâ\x80\x99ve Got Mail (1998) Mistress America (2015) The Humans (2021) Scent of a Woman (1992) Home for the Holidays (1995) The Gold Rush (1925) Prisoners (2013) Addams Family Values (1993) If youâ\x80\x99re still in the mood for something spooky after Halloween, Addams Family Values (1993) is the ideal transitional film. The plot isnâ\x80\x99t Thanksgiving-centric, but one scene in particular makes it a great film to watch around the holiday. While reenacting the first Thanksgiving at camp, Wednesday Addams breaks from the script and delivers a speech listing the injustices Native Americans have endured since the pilgrims arrived. The Last Waltz (1978) This legendary documentary not only chronicles the history of The Band, but also captures their final concert, which took place on Thanksgiving Day, November 25, 1976. They were joined by special guests like Bob Dylan , Joni Mitchell, Muddy Waters, Ringo Starr, and Neil Young. On top of featuring one of the greatest musical lineups of all time, the flick was also the first of many collaborations between The Band frontman Robbie Robertson and director Martin Scorsese . A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving (1973) isnâ\x80\x99t quite as iconic as Itâ\x80\x99s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966) or A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965), but itâ\x80\x99s still a seasonal classic. Watching it ahead of Thanksgiving may make you feel better about your own family dramas.Â Scent of a Woman (1992) In Scent of a Woman , Chris Oâ\x80\x99Donnell plays a student who accepts a job to spend his Thanksgiving break looking after a blind, retired Lieutenant Colonel and alcoholic played by Al Pacino . Holly Hunter plays a recently-unemployed single mom, and Robert Downey Jr. , Anne Bancroft, and Claire Daines fill out the ensemble cast. The best Spidey villains have, obviously, been featured heavily in the live-action films. Whether it's in the Sam Raimi trilogy, the Marc Webb duology, or the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Peter Parker has faced some extremely powerful villains throughout his cinematic career. If the Wall-Crawler beat his foes right off the bat, then audiences wouldn't have entertaining movies to go see. The hero will always get his butt whooped by his villains at some point in the story, because he can't win every fight. Thus, Spidey has had some pretty rough beatings across the years, but who's given him the worst —physically and non-physically? Whether they've killed the love of his life or almost killed him in an intense hand-to-hand battle, Spidey's villains have always given him a run for his money. 12 The Rhino (Paul Giamatti) Paul Giamatti as The Rhino in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 Image via Sony Pictures Releasing People were incredibly excited when they saw the walking wrecking ball known as The Rhino ( Paul Giamatti ) in the trailer for The Amazing Spider-Man 2 . Facing off with such a gigantic foe makes for a perfect David and Goliath-type story for the Web-Slinger, which always leads to great fight scenes. Unfortunately for Rhino fans, he doesn't affect Spider-Man ( Andrew Garfield ) in the slightest. In all fairness, this version of The Rhino shoots some missiles at Spider-Man in the one scene where his armor appears, which also happens to be the final scene of The Amazing Spider-Man 2 . The two don't even touch each other, with the film ending on a cliffhanger, implying that they were about to fight. Pretty disappointing, honestly, but it is what it is. 11 Harry Osborn (James Franco) Harry Osborn on a glider stopping in mid-air in Spider-Man 3 Image via Sony Pictures Entertainment The conflict between Peter Parker ( Tobey Maguire ) and Harry Osborn ( James Franco ) was set up and built upon ever since the end of the first Spider-Man film, when Harry vowed to make Spider-Man pay for what he did to his dad. Obviously, this meant that the two best friends were going to meet some heavy conflict eventually, and it all came to a climax in the trilogy-capper , Spider-Man 3 . At the start of Spider-Man 3 , Harry takes on the mantle of his father's persona, the Green Goblin—commonly called New Goblin outside of the film—to kill Peter once and for all. Driven mad by vengeance and anger, the fight he has with Pete after Mary Jane Watson's ( Kirsten Dunst ) play is intense and fast-paced. However, it is the only time he faces off with his ex-best pal, and this Goblin Jr. doesn't beat Spidey much , being taken down swiftly. 10 Shocker ( Bokeem Woodbine) Herman Schultz scheming in in Spider-Man: Homecoming Image via Sony Pictures Releasing In the MCU, Shocker ( Bokeem Woodbine ) is a pretty underrated Spider-Man villain . He faces off with the hero ( Tom Holland ) only once, but he actually really smacks Spidey around. Shocker punches Spidey so hard that he flies through a bus , before hitting him with another. Peter tries his best, but getting hit by a full school bus didn't do his brain any favors. In fact, the arachnid is about to be taken down until Ned Leeds ( Jacob Batalon ) comes in for the save, using one of the hero's web shooters to stop Shocker from killing his pal. Despite being just a guy with some punching tech, Shocker really smacks Spider-Man around and deserves to make a bigger and better comeback. 9 The Lizard (Rhys Ifans) The Lizard from The Amazing Spider-Man Image via Sony Pictures Releasing When thinking about it, it's pretty understandable that a gigantic mutated lizard man would be someone to kick around a superhero pretty well. While The Amazing Spider-Man let a lot of fans down with its depiction of The Lizard ( Rhys Ifans ), he still gets some good licks on the Wall-Crawler. In the comics, Lizard is typically more savage and brutal, which is missing in his live-action appearances. However, whenever he faces off with Spider-Man, the Lizard never really gets beaten , aside from his retreat in the fight at Midtown High School. The grotesque villain runs away from the bridge because the serum is running out, and Spider-Man escapes their conflict when in the sewers. In fact, the Lizard only loses the fight on the rooftop because Peter beats him to the punch in stopping his plans. 8 The Vulture (Michael Keaton) Vulture smiling while holding a knife in Spider-Man: Homecoming. Image via Sony Pictures Releasing Something Spider-Man has over most of his villains is his agility and ability to swing around and take to the skies. What happens when a villain arises who practically owns the skies? Vulture ( Michael Keaton ) was the perfect villain to kick off Spider-Man's solo career in the MCU, being a lethal threat, but not big enough for the likes of Iron Man ( Robert Downey Jr. ) to notice. Thus, Spidey is the only person who can take the bad bird down. His talons can rip into Spider-Man, his wings can snap his web threads, and his speed allows him to catch the hero off guard, as it happens during their final confrontation on the beach. The Vulture beats Holland's Peter multiple times . The villain gets the Wall-Crawler trapped in the damage control facility in their first interaction, rips the ferry in half (leaving Spider-Man to deal with it), and drops an entire rooftop on him in Act Three. He's not as fatal to Spidey as other live-action villains , but he is not to be sneezed at, either. 7 Venom (Topher Grace) Venom preparing a claw attack in Spider-Man 3 Image via Sony Pictures Releasing Despite being one of the less-appreciated aspects of Spider-Man 3 , Venom ( Topher Grace ) actually kicks the crap out of Spidey all across the construction site they fight in during the final battle. Not only does Venom not set off the Wall-Crawler's Spider-Sense, but he's just as fast (if not faster) and just as strong . The best way to describe Venom is Spider-Man is he was evil , which is a horrific thing to think about. Had it not been for Harry Osborn's sacrifice to save him, Peter would have most likely died at the hands of Venom . The symbiote may have only fought Spidey once, but he makes his mark and ensures himself as a memorable villain for reasons that aren't exclusively bad. Venim is ruthless as he almost kills Peter, almost kills Mary Jane, and unfortunately takes Harry's life. 6 Sandman ( Thomas Haden Church) Thomas Haden Church as Sandman in Spider-Man 3 Image via Sony Pictures Releasing The ability to absorb all of the sand in the area surrounding you, turning you into a gigantic, multiple-story monster, is pretty dang overpowered. Being made of sand means that the Sandman ( Thomas Haden Church ) is a tough cookie to crack, as physical punches don't really affect him. Sandman, with the help of Venom, was mere moments away from taking Spider-Man's life by simply using one hand and slamming down on him. He literally stood there and hit Spider-Man like a whack-a-mole, barely breaking a sweat . Being able to kill someone with that much ease is freaky, and if not for Harry Osborn, the Sandman would have squashed Spidey like one does to an actual spider. 5 Electro (Jamie Foxx) Image via Sony Pictures Releasing While he gets a lot of flak, thanks to The Amazing Spider-Man 2 's overall weak rep, Electro ( Jamie Foxx ) is a pretty dang powerful villain, and the movie doesn't shy away from that. Electro can zap Spidey away with a mere touch and has the ability to control anything with electricity. Not to mention, his electrical blasts are so powerful, they evaporated civilians in Times Square during his first fight with Spider-Man. The power of electricity is extremely strong; after all, it's a basic law of the world. It doesn't take a lot of electricity to shut down the human body completely, and while Spider-Man has an enhanced physicality, even he can't take a bolt of lightning to the chest and just walk it off. This vulnerability is proven throughout the entire final fight, in which Spidey's plans to stop Electro would not have been possible without Gwen Stacy ( Emma Stone ) there. Even so, the arachnid gets mere seconds away from frying his whole body while trying to hold his webs together. Before Gwen arrives, Spider-Man is at Electro's mercy and is getting his world rocked for almost the entire fight . 4 Doctor Otto Octavius (Alfred Molina) There's no questioning that Doctor Otto Octavius ( Alfred Molina ), aka Doctor Octopus, is the villain of one of the best superhero movies, Spider-Man 2 , which would make him one of the de facto best Spider-Man villains. Alongside that reputation, Doc Ock also gave the Wall-Crawler several major beatings. Pete only bests Otto in battle once , at the end of the movie, after being beaten or having the villain escape in the previous ones. Doc Ock almost fully crushes Spidey's head like a watermelon in the bank fight, almost kills Aunt May ( Rosemary Harris ) , and almost impales the hero if not for her interference. In the iconic train battle, Spidey gets smacked around until Otto forces him to stay behind to keep the train from crashing, causing Peter to extend himself to a limit that could have easily killed him. He also captures the Web-Slinger, something that not many have done. Not to forget, in the film's extended cut, Spider-Man 2.1 , he even puts the hero in front of an oncoming train , which he gets hit by. 3 Harry Osborn (Dane DeHaan) Dane DeHaan as Green Goblin in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 Image via Sony Pictures Releasing Another negatively-received villain from the live-action franchises is yet another Harry Osborn ( Dane DeHaan ), this time from The Amazing Spider-Man universe. Appearing pretty much out of nowhere after the final Electro fight in The Amazing Spider-Man 2 , this Harry-Goblin puts up quite a fight against Peter when he brings him and Gwen Stacy to the clock tower for a close-quarters battle. Not only is it an extremely tough battle, but this Goblin Jr. beats Peter in a way that no other villain has: he takes the life of Gwen Stacy by holding the arachnid down and forcing the web holding her to snap. This action is so impactful—so terribly ruinous—that it puts Spider-Man out of commission for months. From sweeping fantasy epics to gritty crime sagas the best movie trilogies represent storytelling at its most ambitious and satisfying. These aren\'t just three films released one after the other – they\'re carefully constructed narrative arcs that build worlds, explore core themes, and deliver emotional payoffs that single films simply can\'t match. The greatest film trilogies work because they understand the classic three-act storytelling structure: the introduction, the escalation, and the resolution. Whether it\'s watching a young farmboy become a Jedi Knight across a galaxy far, far away, following a teenager\'s adventures through time and space, or witnessing the rise and fall of a mafia family across generations, the best trilogy movies give us room to breathe, grow attached, and experience genuine transformation alongside their characters. From the action-packed thrills of globe-trotting archaeologists and time-travelling DeLoreans to intimate character studies from auteur filmmakers, movie trilogies span every genre and filmmaking approach imaginable. What makes certain trilogies endure while others fade? Sometimes it\'s the visionary director who maps out all three chapters from the start. Other times, it\'s the unexpected alchemy of a sequel that deepens what came before, transforming a standalone hit into something greater. And occasionally, it\'s the cultural moment they capture – the way the best trilogies of all time become iconic texts for entire generations, their quotes embedded in our conversations, their themes debated for decades. Like we said: it’s the magic number. How We Chose The Best Film Trilogies Compiling a definitive ranking of the best trilogies was never going to be a simple task. We started by asking you, Empire \'s passionate readers, to vote for your favourite all-time movie trilogies. Thousands of you responded, championing everything from pure three-film series untouched by prequels or sequels, to specific trios within longer franchises, to triptychs that were intended to be evaluated as a threesome even if they don’t share the same cast or characters. Where a coherent narrative across three films existed, we counted it – which is why you\'ll find certain trilogies here even when fourth or fifth instalments later emerged. Once your votes were in, we turned to Empire \'s experienced team of critics and contributors, asking them to weigh in with their expertise on the artistic merit, cultural impact, and lasting influence of each trilogy. We evaluated how well each trilogy functions as a complete narrative – does the third film stick the landing? Does the middle chapter avoid the sophomore slump? Do all three films come together to create something greater than the sum of their parts? After much heated discussion, countless rewatches, and vigorous debate about everything from superhero standouts to South Korean revenge thrillers, from comedy spoofs to zombie horrors , we arrived at our final ranking. Whether you\'re a devotee of groundbreaking sci-fi, animated classics or international arthouse cinema, you\'ll find something to love – and, probably, something to argue about – in our rundown of the greatest film trios ever made. So here, without further ado, is Empire \'s official ranking of the 33 (see what we did there?) best movie trilogies of all time... 33. The Jersey Trilogy (1994 – 1997) Clerks (1994) | Mallrats (1995) | Chasing Amy (1997) Streaming on: NOW | Apple TV Director: Kevin Smith Starring: Brian O\'Halloran, Jeff Anderson, Jason Mewes, Kevin Smith, Shannon Doherty, Jeremy London, Claire Forlani, Jason Lee, Ben Affleck, Joey Lauren Adams, Ethan Suplee A loose trilogy, this, but we\'re assuming you readers felt this list was a little light on profanity and needed some explicit discussion of oral sex to balance out the selection. And on that basis, it\'s hard to surpass Kevin Smith\'s first three films: a more grounded group than his follow-ons and, in the case of Chasing Amy especially, a near perfect mix of foul-mouthery, far too in-depth geek discussions and warm heartedness. Smith hasn\'t surpassed Amy yet, but we can only hope he keeps trying to at least equal it. It just goes to show you don\'t need fallen angels, chimps or even Rosario Dawson to make a great movie. Weakest link? Mallrats , which didn\'t deserve the kicking it got on release, but is also by far the weakest of the three. Fun fact: Wondering where the letters in the Clerks logo came from? Well, C is from Cosmopolitan, L is from Life, E is from Rolling Stone, R is from Ruffles potato chips, K is from Clark Bar and S is from a Goobers box. Hannibal Lecter Trilogy (1991 – 2002) The Silence of the Lambs (1991 ) | Hannibal (2001) | Red Dragon (2002) Streaming on: Apple TV | NOW | Sky Directors: Jonathan Demme, Ridley Scott, Brett Ratner Starring: Anthony Hopkins, Jodie Foster, Ted Levine, Scott Glenn, Julianne Moore, Ray Liotta, Gary Oldman, Giancarlo Giannini, Edward Norton, Ralph Fiennes, Harvey Keitel, Mary Louise Parker, Philip Seymour Hoffman Anthony Hopkins\' performance as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence Of The Lambs is the shortest ever to win Best (leading) Actor at the Oscars. He\'s only on screen for 16 minutes, but such is his domination of the film that you\'d swear it was two or three times that. It\'s no wonder that studios kept trying to recapture that lightning in a bottle, recruiting cinema\'s best ever villain for a sequel and a prequel (there\'s another prequel, not starring Hopkins and not included here) which saw diminishing returns but still benefitted from that uncanny, barely-blinking performance. So why not settle down with a nice Chianti and enjoy the trio in full? Weakest link? The first film is undoubtedly the strongest. Hannibal suffers from the world\'s worst last act (in fairness, hamstrung by the source novel and improving slightly on it), whereas Red Dragon is a decent if unexceptional thriller. Fun fact: The Silence Of The Lambs is one of only three films ever to win all "Big Five" Oscars: Best Film, Director, Screenplay, Actor and Actress. The Ingmar Bergman Trilogy (1961 – 1963) Through A Glass Darkly (1961) | Winter Light (1962) | The Silence (1963) Director: Ingmar Bergman Starring: Harriet Andersson, Gunnar Bjornstrand, Max Von Sydow, Ingrid Thulin, Gunnel Lindblom, Jorgen Lindstrom Although it\'s too much of a stretch to call it Bergman\'s franchise, this early \'60s troika are exquisite chamber pieces built around themes of sanity, madness and the wavering of religious faith, thus earning the right to be called a trilogy. Through A Glass Darkly charts a family\'s descent into madness on a remote island. Winter Light sees a pastor in a spiritual meltdown and might be the most grim film Bergman ever made (and that\'s saying something). The Silence ticks all the arthouse boxes, depicting lesbianism, a troupe of dwarves, symbolism and Ingrid Thulin dying of tuberculosis; it was a surprise hit due its explicit (for the time) rumpy-pumpy scenes. Each film is marked by eerie settings, minimal dialogue, great Sven Nykvist photography and superb performances from Bergman\'s stock company. Weakest link? Although it won the Best Foreign Language Film Oscar, Through A Glass Darkly is the least affecting of the three. Still compelling stuff, though. Fun fact: When Kabi Laretei (Bergman\'s wife at the time) saw Winter Lights for the first time, she said, "Ingmar, it\'s a masterpiece. But it\'s a dreary masterpiece." 30. We\'re still not sure it\'s possible to make silicone masks that convincing though. Weakest link? Mission: Impossible II , which takes the whole people-peeling-off-their-faces thing to ridiculous levels, and definitely places style (and floppy hair) over substance. Weakest link? Well, parts four, five and six actually; the original three are all rather brilliant. MVP for the series is Noomi Rapace, a stunningly well-cast Lisbeth, and a true heroine for the 21st century. Weakest link? Fun fact: Dolph Lundgren was offered the part of German giant Ronald Niederman, and had he taken it it would have been his first role in his native Swedish. 26. Weakest link? By several country miles, Blade: Trinity . With the exception of Ryan Reynolds\' delivery of one of cinema\'s greatest all-time insults, it has very little to recommend it. The Austin Powers Trilogy (1997 – 2002) Austin Powers: International Man Of Mystery (1997) | Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me (1999) | Austin Powers In Goldmember (2002) Streaming on: Prime Video | ITVX | Apple TV Director: Jay Roach Starring: Mike Myers, Elizabeth Hurley, Michael York, Mimi Rogers, Robert Wagner, Seth Green, Mindy Sterling, Heather Graham, Rob Lowe, Verne Troyer, Beyonce, Michael Caine, Fred Savage After Wayne, but happily long before The Love Guru, there was Austin Powers and his wonderfully mediocre arch-nemesis, Dr Evil. Mike Myers\' dual performances may have paled from over-familiarity and a million pub mimics, but looked at with fresh eyes, they\'re still genius. See where they came in our lists of the best animated movies , best kids movies , and Pixar movie ranking . 3. Back To The Future Trilogy (1985 – 1990) Back To The Future (1985) | Back To The Future Part II (1989) | Back To The Future Part III (1990) Streaming on: Netflix | Prime Video Director: Robert Zemeckis Starring: Michael J. Fox, Christopher Lloyd, Crispin Glover, Lea Thompson, Thomas F. Wilson, Claudia Wells, Elizabeth Shue, Mary Steenbergen Show us a person who doesn\'t like Back To The Future and we\'ll show you a person who is tired of life. The Zemeckis-directed, Spielberg-produced time-travelling tale of Marty McFly races along at, oooh, around 88mph, fuelled by plutonium and Fox\'s career-making, insanely charming performance as an average teen thrust 30 years back in time. Part II was a twisty, turny paradox-spinning puzzler, followed by a gorgeous mix of old West and space age in Part III . Consistently fun, funny and about as good an adventure romp as you could wish for, there\'s a reason that this is still wildly popular decades on. Weakest link? Funnily enough, conventional wisdom at the time tended to rate the second film lowest (as reflected by Empire \'s reviews) but nowadays you\'ll find more people slagging off the third. It all smacks of looking a gift horse in the mouth to us though. Fun fact: Once upon a time, the time machine was going to be a fridge. Spielberg and Zemeckis nixed the idea because they were worried about kids copying the movie and getting trapped in old fridges. Read Empire \'s reviews of Back To The Future , Part II and Part III . 2. The Original Star Wars Trilogy (1977 – 1983) Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope (1977) | Star Wars: Episode V - The Empire Strikes Back (1980) | Star Wars: Episode VI - Return of the Jedi (1983) Streaming on: Disney+ Directors: George Lucas, Irvin Kershner, Richard Marquand Starring: Mark Hamill, Harrison Ford, Carrie Fisher, Alec Guinness, Peter Cushing, Anthony Daniels, Peter Mayhew, Kenny Baker, David Prowse, James Earl Jones, Billy Dee Williams, Jeremy Bulloch George Lucas\' opening space-opera salvo changed the filmmaking landscape, energised a generation and set an impossible standard for any sequel. Irvin Kershner\'s sequel , with Lucas overseeing, delivered something even bigger and better, and also gave us perhaps the most famous twist in cinema history. And the third, while it may have cutesy teddy bears taking down an Empire, also has a series of fantastic action scenes, from the fight with the Rancor to the lightsaber battle on the Death Star – itself under attack from outside. The original batch of Star Wars movies is a triple-whammy that has spawned imitators, prequels, endless other media permutations and even a religion. How many trilogies can claim that? Weakest link? Most of the fanboys would have you believe it\'s Jedi , but that\'s got some of the trilogy\'s best bits in it, and – whatever they claim – no one hated the Ewoks, even when they were a kid. Fun fact: Pop quiz, hotshot. Who has the last line in New Hope? Answer: Chewbacca. Read Empire \'s reviews of A New Hope , The Empire Strikes Back and Return Of The Jedi . 1. The Lord Of The Rings (2001 – 2003) The Lord Of The Rings: The Fellowship Of The Ring (2001) | The Lord Of The Rings: The Two Towers (2002) | The Lord Of The Rings: The Return Of The King (2003) Streaming on: Apple TV | Prime Video Director: Peter Jackson Starring: Elijah Wood, Viggo Mortensen, Ian McKellen, Cate Blanchett, Sean Astin, Sean Bean, John Rhys-Davies, Christopher Lee, Andy Serkis, Orlando Bloom, Dominic Monahan, Billy Boyd, Liv Tyler, Hugo Weaving, Miranda Otto, Karl Urban, David Wenham, Bernard Hill, Ian Holm, Brad Dourif, John Noble Peter Jackson\'s stunning trilogy, filmed back-to-back and released in the form of Christmas presents for three consecutive years, just pipped Star Wars to the top of the poll. Why? Well, there\'s the painstaking attention to detail (characters even had their coats-of-arms emblazoned on the never-seen linings of their costumes for maximum authenticity), New Zealand scenery so breathtaking you can feel the wind on your face, the pitch-perfect casting and the huge-scale effects. In the end, however, it all comes down to friendship, and fellowship, and a struggle against the odds (or, if you will, orcs). It\'s the fact that Peter Jackson was able to keep his eye on the emotion even while the spectacle swirled around him that makes these three films such a stunning achievement – and why all three of them appear in our official list of the 100 greatest movies of all time . Weakest link? There really isn\'t one – although a few people gripe about Return Of The King \'s extended endings. Fun fact: While Return Of The King is tied with Titanic and Ben-Hur for the Most Oscars For A Single Film record (that\'d be 11), it\'s notable for winning all the Academy Awards it was nominated for, which neither of the others managed to do. The trailer depicts the two matriarchs bargaining over land ownership "not for greed, but for survival". View 2 Images Gillian Anderson stars as Constance Van Ness (Image: NETFLIX) \u200c The Western will debut on Netflix on December 4. Enthusiasts of programmes like Yellowstone will be captivated by the themes of family and their fierce determination to safeguard what belongs to them. The teaser cautions "some bonds are stronger than blood" as audiences discover the extremes these families will pursue for survival. \u200c Viewers rushed to the YouTube comments to express their opinions, with @megalon73 declaring: "Gillian Anderson and Lena Headey in the same film together. I\'m down to watch." @iliyassarsembaev remarked: "Wow! For the sake of these two women in one film, I will definitely watch it!" @VictorOkoli-xr4vv wrote: "Now this is how you do a trailer." \u200c View 2 Images The Abandons will air on Netflix (Image: NETFLIX) @jamien368 commended the leading stars\' acting, adding: "I swear, if Lena Headey doesn\'t win an Emmy this time." A user named @magicalmousers expressed their excitement, stating: "That\'s going to be one of the most epic bad*** Western shows ever. I can\'t wait." Article continues below Lena Headey portrays Fiona Nolan, a deeply religious Irish woman unable to have children, who seeks to create a family by adopting four orphans. In contrast, Gillian Anderson takes on the role of Constance Van Ness, a character who poses a threat to her newly acquired home in Oregon. The Abandons is set to premiere on Netflix on December 4. Netflix has seen success in Western TV, with titles like American Primeval and Territory finding acclaim. It is not surprising that Netflix aims to continue this trend by creating inventive and binge-worthy Western content on its platform with the Kurt Sutter (Sons of Anarchy, Mayans M.C.)–created show The Abandons . Moreover, the series is set to release in December 2025, ensuring the year ends on a high note for the Western TV fandom, with some already touting it as the perfect replacement for Yellowstone . The recent announcement of The Abandons has undoubtedly made an impression. Whether it\'s from the trailer that depicts a picturesque yet brutal Old West setting, the stage for a battle between a greedy land developer and a community, or the phenomenal casting of Gillian Anderson and Lena Headey, there is a lot to get excited about as we approach its release. Still, there are many details Western fans will be looking for before the series\' release. Here, we will cover everything we know about The Abandons , including the cast, plot, and when it will be available to stream . What We Know About the Plot of \'The Abandons\' Netflix Set in Washington Territory in 1854, in the fictional town of Jasper Hollow, The Abandons follows two different matriarchs from different backgrounds into conflict : Constance Van Ness (Gillian Anderson), a strong-willed philanthropist who will stop at nothing to continue to grow the mining business fortune she inherited from her husband, and Fiona Nolan (Lena Headey) a faith-driven woman who has made a family of outcasts and souls on the fringe of society, who stands firm against pressure to leave the cattle ranch she built in silver-rich Jasper Hollow under pressure from the Van Ness family. The two families become violently intertwined over a long-hidden secret, land ownership, and a star-crossed romance. In an interview with Tudum , executive producer Christopher Keyser explained that the first chapter of the series delves into a heated rivalry. “This first chapter of The Abandons is a classic American story — the frontier, two families both at war and in love with each other, [and] a battle over who owns the land and who makes the rules” In the same article, Keyser expressed excitement for the project and the twists and turns it will take audiences through, led by its phenomenal cast: “In the middle of murder and revenge and a bit of illicit romance, we get to explore questions we never seem to get away from: What makes a family? How do you stay good in a bad world? And would you change who you are and what you believe in to protect what you love? But in this case, we do it all through the eyes of Lena Headey and Gillian Anderson, as two widowed matriarchs battling to survive. And that … is really something to watch.” Whether the show will have subsequent seasons remains unconfirmed. However, the first season promises nail-biting, addictive action and drama, making it a perfect replacement for fans feeling the void left by the end of Yellowstone . \'The Abandons\' Comes With a Phenomenal Cast and Crew Netflix The Abandons is created by Kurt Sutter, who has amassed an impressive career in TV, having previously worked on The Shield , Sons of Anarchy , The Bastard Executioner , and Mayans M.C . However, Sutter exited the project weeks before it wrapped ( via Entertainment Weekly ) — neither Netflix nor Sutter commented on the exit. Sutter is credited with the show\'s inaugural episode, with Otto Bathurst and Rob Askins taking over for the rest of the series; there is officially no showrunner. While there were issues behind the scenes, Sutter\'s involvement ideally sets the groundwork to carry the series forward. Notably, director Otto Bathurst has worked on several series, including Black Mirror , His Dark Materials , and Halo , and brings his expertise to carry the inaugural season past its first episode. What will stand out for most is the lead cast of The Abandons , with Lena Headey as Fiona Nolan and Gillian Anderson as Constance Van Ness . Fan favorite Gillian Anderson entered pop culture through her role as Dana Scully in The X-Files , but has remained a consistent force in TV and film, with notable roles in Sex Education and Tron: Ares . Lena Headey, to most, is best known for her role in Game of Thrones as Cersei Lannister . This is the first time Nolan and Anderson will be working together, and the two as opposing forces is a welcome prospect. The series is also backed by a phenomenal supporting cast, including familiar faces from Netflix staples such as Marc Menchaca ( Ozark ) and Katelyn Wells ( Ginny & Georgia ), while actors from past Sutter-created shows also appear: Brían F. O’Byrne ( The Bastard Executioner ), Clayton Cardenas ( Mayans M.C. ), and Michael Ornstein ( Sons of Anarchy ). There will be 10 episodes, all available on the same day . Netflix subscribers are certainly going to have their hands full of content in December. The platform is bringing holiday movies and series, including the Netflix original Christmas series Man vs. Baby starring Rowan Atkinson. Additionally, fans will be anticipating the final episodes of Stranger Things alongside the return of favorites like Emily in Paris for its fifth season. Yet, The Abandons is perfectly placed at the start of the month, perfect for a binge session before getting two wrapped up in seasonal viewings. The trailer reveals the two matriarchs negotiating over land ownership "not for greed, but for survival". Fans of shows like Yellowstone will be captivated by the themes of familial bonds and their fierce determination to safeguard what\'s theirs. The teaser ominously warns "some bonds are stronger than blood", hinting at the extreme measures the families will take to ensure their survival. Viewers were quick to share their excitement in the YouTube comments section. @megalon73 enthused: "Gillian Anderson and Lena Headey in the same film together. View 2 Images The Abandons will air on Netflix (Image: NETFLIX) \u200c Meanwhile, @jamien368 lauded the performances of the lead actresses, adding: "I swear, if Lena Headey doesn\'t win an Emmy this time." Twitter user @magicalmousers excitedly stated: "That\'s going to be one of the most epic bad*** Western shows ever. I can\'t wait." Lena Headey portrays Fiona Nolan, a deeply religious Irish woman who is unable to conceive. She attempts to create a family by adopting four orphans. Article continues below In contrast, Gillian Anderson takes on the role of Constance Van Ness, who poses a threat to take over her newly acquired home in Oregon. The Abandons will be available on Netflix from 4 December. Netflix has seen success in Western TV, with titles like American Primeval and Territory finding acclaim. It is not surprising that Netflix aims to continue this trend by creating inventive and binge-worthy Western content on its platform with the Kurt Sutter (Sons of Anarchy, Mayans M.C.)–created show The Abandons . Moreover, the series is set to release in December 2025, ensuring the year ends on a high note for the Western TV fandom, with some already touting it as the perfect replacement for Yellowstone . The recent announcement of The Abandons has undoubtedly made an impression. Whether it\'s from the trailer that depicts a picturesque yet brutal Old West setting, the stage for a battle between a greedy land developer and a community, or the phenomenal casting of Gillian Anderson and Lena Headey, there is a lot to get excited about as we approach its release. Still, there are many details Western fans will be looking for before the series\' release. Here, we will cover everything we know about The Abandons , including the cast, plot, and when it will be available to stream . What We Know About the Plot of \'The Abandons\' Netflix Set in Washington Territory in 1854, in the fictional town of Jasper Hollow, The Abandons follows two different matriarchs from different backgrounds into conflict : Constance Van Ness (Gillian Anderson), a strong-willed philanthropist who will stop at nothing to continue to grow the mining business fortune she inherited from her husband, and Fiona Nolan (Lena Headey) a faith-driven woman who has made a family of outcasts and souls on the fringe of society, who stands firm against pressure to leave the cattle ranch she built in silver-rich Jasper Hollow under pressure from the Van Ness family. The two families become violently intertwined over a long-hidden secret, land ownership, and a star-crossed romance. In an interview with Tudum , executive producer Christopher Keyser explained that the first chapter of the series delves into a heated rivalry. “This first chapter of The Abandons is a classic American story — the frontier, two families both at war and in love with each other, [and] a battle over who owns the land and who makes the rules” In the same article, Keyser expressed excitement for the project and the twists and turns it will take audiences through, led by its phenomenal cast: “In the middle of murder and revenge and a bit of illicit romance, we get to explore questions we never seem to get away from: What makes a family? How do you stay good in a bad world? And would you change who you are and what you believe in to protect what you love? But in this case, we do it all through the eyes of Lena Headey and Gillian Anderson, as two widowed matriarchs battling to survive. And that … is really something to watch.” Whether the show will have subsequent seasons remains unconfirmed. However, the first season promises nail-biting, addictive action and drama, making it a perfect replacement for fans feeling the void left by the end of Yellowstone . \'The Abandons\' Comes With a Phenomenal Cast and Crew Netflix The Abandons is created by Kurt Sutter, who has amassed an impressive career in TV, having previously worked on The Shield , Sons of Anarchy , The Bastard Executioner , and Mayans M.C . However, Sutter exited the project weeks before it wrapped ( via Entertainment Weekly ) — neither Netflix nor Sutter commented on the exit. Sutter is credited with the show\'s inaugural episode, with Otto Bathurst and Rob Askins taking over for the rest of the series; there is officially no showrunner. While there were issues behind the scenes, Sutter\'s involvement ideally sets the groundwork to carry the series forward. Notably, director Otto Bathurst has worked on several series, including Black Mirror , His Dark Materials , and Halo , and brings his expertise to carry the inaugural season past its first episode. What will stand out for most is the lead cast of The Abandons , with Lena Headey as Fiona Nolan and Gillian Anderson as Constance Van Ness . Fan favorite Gillian Anderson entered pop culture through her role as Dana Scully in The X-Files , but has remained a consistent force in TV and film, with notable roles in Sex Education and Tron: Ares . Lena Headey, to most, is best known for her role in Game of Thrones as Cersei Lannister . This is the first time Nolan and Anderson will be working together, and the two as opposing forces is a welcome prospect. The series is also backed by a phenomenal supporting cast, including familiar faces from Netflix staples such as Marc Menchaca ( Ozark ) and Katelyn Wells ( Ginny & Georgia ), while actors from past Sutter-created shows also appear: Brían F. O’Byrne ( The Bastard Executioner ), Clayton Cardenas ( Mayans M.C. ), and Michael Ornstein ( Sons of Anarchy ). Complete cast list of The Abandons : Lena Headey as Fiona Nolan Gillian Anderson as Constance Van Ness Brían F. There will be 10 episodes, all available on the same day . Netflix subscribers are certainly going to have their hands full of content in December. The platform is bringing holiday movies and series, including the Netflix original Christmas series Man vs. Baby starring Rowan Atkinson. Additionally, fans will be anticipating the final episodes of Stranger Things alongside the return of favorites like Emily in Paris for its fifth season. Yet, The Abandons is perfectly placed at the start of the month, perfect for a binge session before getting two wrapped up in seasonal viewings.
